title: Hair's breadth
hookLine: the poem: a hair's breadth of difference and heaven and earth are set apart

lines: THE WHEEL, A HAIR OFF TRUE.
cards: A ship leaves harbor with its wheel turned the smallest bit off true. From the dock, nobody could see it. A day out, the coast still looks right.
But keep sailing, across a whole ocean, and that ship comes ashore on a different coast from the one it meant to reach. The turn was tiny. The distance it opens is not.
Yesterday's poem has a line built on exactly this shape: the smallest gap, the largest distance.

teach.b: In paraphrase, the Xinxin Ming says: if there is the slightest difference, a hair's breadth, then heaven and earth are set apart. It comes a few lines after the opening, so it isn't a new subject.
It's the same warning about picking and choosing, now with a picture of how big the cost can grow.

teach.h: NOT A CALL TO BE PERFECT.
teach.b: It can sound like a call to be exacting: a hair's breadth off and you've failed. But that reading turns the line into one more round of picking and choosing, right against wrong, perfect against flawed.
The difference the poem means is the split the mind makes between what is here and what it wants instead. That split usually opens very small.

teach.h: THE FIRST FLICKER OF A LEAN.
teach.b: A name lights up on your phone and, before you read a word, there's a flicker. Ugh. Or a flicker of yes, this one I like.
No story yet, no argument, just a lean. That lean is the hair's breadth. Why heaven and earth?
The poem pairs the smallest thing it can name with the largest. It isn't threatening anyone.

It's describing distance. A tiny lean, held and fed, tilts the whole conversation, then the whole relationship, the way a hair off on the wheel puts a ship on another coast. And the line has a gentler side.
If the gap begins as a hair, it can also be noticed while it is still only a hair wide.

how: Zen and Chan teachers often quote this line of the Xinxin Ming in talks to point at how quickly a small preference becomes a large separation, and students use it as a reminder during sitting.

o: the tiniest lean of liking or disliking
an exact standard that leaves no room for error
a narrow escape from danger, a near miss

p: a ship's wheel, a hair off

s: the line is a call to get every detail perfect
that reading turns it into more picking and choosing; the difference it means is the lean of like and dislike.
the line continues the poem's warning about picking and choosing
it follows the opening, then shows how large the cost of a small split can grow.
the poem treats tiny differences as harmless
a hair's breadth, it says, is enough to set heaven and earth apart.

games.q: a name lights up on your phone, and before you read a word there's a tiny 'ugh'. according to today's line, where does the split begin?
o: only if the message turns out rude
games.why: the hair's breadth is the first lean, before any story. the poem's point is that the distance grows from there, and that it can be noticed while it's still small.

practice: Let sounds, thoughts and sensations come as they come, and watch for the very first flicker as each one arrives: a slight lean toward it, or a slight lean away, before any story.
When you catch one, name it quietly, lean, and let it pass.

wordCard.voice: Hair's breadth. In the Xinxin Ming, the slightest difference, the tiny lean of liking and disliking, which sets heaven and earth apart. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (haoli): 'a hair's breadth', the smallest gap, set against heaven and earth in the poem's line.

carryVoice: Your line: a hair's breadth. Small enough to miss, and small enough to catch. Same time tomorrow.
